growth_story.headline: Oil lifted Chad's income per person in the 2000s; since the 2012 peak, oil shocks, ageing fields and regional crises have left it 14.1 percent lower.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Chad shrank by 1.5 percent a year from 1990 to 2000, an era the sources we read say little about. From 2001 to 2008 it grew 7.5 percent a year, as oil production began in 2003 and peaked the next year; income per person jumped 27.8 percent in 2004 alone. Since 2009 growth has averaged -0.2 percent a year: income per person peaked in 2012, the 2014-15 oil price crash brought recession in 2016 and 2017, and another recession followed in 2020. By 2025 income per person was 14.1 percent below the 2012 peak, about where it first was in 2005, and over 2016 to 2025 it fell 1.2 percent a year on average. Recent sources add ageing oil fields, a large inflow of refugees from Sudan's war and a long political transition to the story.

threads.title: Oil arrives, then peaks early
threads.text: Oil production began in 2003 and output from the first fields peaked the following year, which matches the burst of growth in 2004 and 2005. The World Bank describes growth over three decades as dominated by oil, and production from the original fields declined soon after the peak.

threads.title: The 2014 oil price crash
threads.text: When oil prices fell in 2014 and 2015, Chad slid into recession, and income per person fell 7.1 percent in 2016 and 4.8 percent in 2017. The IMF says earlier gains in health, education and poverty reduction have stalled since that shock.

threads.text: War in Sudan has pushed a very large number of refugees into eastern Chad, and more arrived in 2025. The sources link the influx to higher food prices and to strain on public services.

threads.title: Ageing oil fields, new mines
threads.text: Output from Chad's maturing oil fields has been falling, and technical problems followed the nationalisation of an operator's assets in 2023. Oil still supplies much of the state's revenue and exports, while gold and copper mining has become a newer source of activity.

threads.title: A long political transition
threads.text: A political transition that began in 2021 ended with senate elections in February 2025. The IMF says the strains of those years brought higher spending and larger budget deficits, and an IMF-supported programme went off track in 2023 before a new arrangement in 2025.

since_last_year.text: Growth picked up. Income per person rose 2.0 percent in 2025 after falling 0.1 percent in 2024. The IMF reported in December 2025 that non-oil revenue came in above projections, and the World Bank says growth in early 2026 came from non-oil activity, especially mining, as gold output rose and copper production began.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Chad
citations.quote: Real GDP grew 3.4 percent year-on-year in Q1 2026, driven by non-oil sectors (+4.1 percent), particularly mining

citations.title: IMF Staff Reaches Staff-Level Agreement with the Chadian Authorities on the First Review under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF)
citations.quote: Non-oil revenues exceeded projections, supported by stronger economic activity and ECF-related tax measures.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe solid growth in total output in 2024 and 2025, yet income per person fell 0.1 percent in 2024 and rose only 2.0 percent in 2025. Rapid population growth, which the World Bank also notes, accounts for much of the gap, so strong headline growth has done little to lift income per person back toward its 2012 peak.
